argument: Compute throughput has historically improved faster than memory access latency and, for many workloads, usable bandwidth. As a result, cache misses, irregular access, and data movement can dominate execution time even when arithmetic units are underutilized.
boundary: The severity depends on locality, working set, hierarchy, prefetching, parallelism, and workload.
High-bandwidth memory and near-memory compute alleviate but do not universally remove the bottleneck.
Latency- and bandwidth-bound behavior must be distinguished.
claim: Compute throughput has historically improved faster than memory access latency and, for many workloads, usable bandwidth. As a result, cache misses, irregular access, and data movement can dominate execution time even when arithmetic units are underutilized.
interpretation: “Memory-bound” should be demonstrated with measured traffic and attainable bandwidth, not inferred from low compute utilization alone.

title: Processor Throughput Can Outrun Memory Latency and Bandwidth, Making Data Access the Bottleneck

argument: Observed values are not direct copies of reality; they are outputs of instruments, calibration models, sampling rules, and operational definitions. A scientific Principle inherits the validity limits of the measurement chain used to instantiate its variables.
boundary: Some measurements are highly standardized and robust across instruments.
Acknowledging theory-ladenness does not imply that all measurements are arbitrary.
Measurement error can be differential and intervention-dependent.

interpretation: Principia should link a Principle to its measurement method and calibration version, especially when the same named variable has multiple operational definitions.
